label: Ch 4 · The bill: what MD costs

scenes.title: The bill: what MD costs
scenes.sub: Time · focus · work · mood · sleep · success fantasies · your pattern
scenes.say: Chapter four. What the loop costs, why success fantasies are the costliest kind, and how your pattern lines up with the evidence.
A recall from chapter three. What belief drives the escape?
scenes.sayA: That the fantasy will repair your mood. In fact, MD is followed by a worse mood the next day.
scenes.a: That fantasy will repair your mood. It's followed by a worse one.

scenes.head: Time: share of waking hours spent daydreaming
scenes.say: Time is the most visible cost. People with MD report spending 57 percent of their waking hours in daydreams, against 16 percent for people without it. Diary participants reported 4.5 hours of active daydreaming in a single day. These are self-estimates, but the gap is enormous.

scenes.head: Focus
scenes.text: I often feel as if I just *cannot turn off my mind*, whether because I need to concentrate in class, go to sleep, or just find some peace.
scenes.note: During MD the mind isn't drifting. It's busy building scenes.
scenes.say: Focus pays next. People with MD report a reduced ability to sustain attention outward, because of the lure of the inner world. One diary participant said: I often feel as if I just cannot turn off my mind, whether because I need to concentrate in class, go to sleep, or just find some peace. Somer stresses that during MD the mind is not drifting. It is focused on creating scenes. It competes directly with your work for the same deliberate attention.

scenes.text: Across 88 samples, more mind-wandering meant worse performance, and the cost was *more pronounced for more complex tasks*.
scenes.note: Scripting, edit decisions and strategy are exactly those tasks
scenes.say: Across 88 samples in the general population, more mind-wandering meant worse task performance, and the cost was more pronounced for more complex tasks. Scripting, editing decisions and business strategy are exactly those complex tasks.

scenes.head: Work and income

items: Lockdown: impaired work and family life
Medical students: weak link to procrastination

scenes.say: Work and income suffer in clinical samples. In Somer's music study, 46 percent were unemployed, and fewer than 15 percent were in a relationship. During lockdown, MD was linked to impaired social, family and work activities. But honestly, no study has objectively measured output, like words written or hours of focused work. In one group of medical students, MD was only weakly linked to procrastination, and their grades were unaffected.

scenes.head: Take this seriously
scenes.text: In 39 people diagnosed by interview, *28%* had attempted suicide. In 2,512 US adults, suspected MD was linked to recent attempts (odds ratio 2.44).
scenes.note: Signals, not predictions about you. If such thoughts come, seek help now.
scenes.say: Mood carries the strongest evidence on direction, and at the severe end there is a signal to take seriously. Among 39 people with interview-diagnosed MD, 28 percent had attempted suicide. In a US panel of 2,512 adults, people flagged for suspected MD were more than twice as likely to have made a recent attempt. These are signals, not predictions about any one person. If thoughts like that ever come, seek help straight away.

scenes.head: Sleep: the surprise
scenes.text: People with MD widely report it ruins sleep. But in a pre-registered diary study of 126 people, MD did *not* predict worse sleep that night.
scenes.note: Poor sleep did predict more mind-wandering the next day
scenes.say: Sleep is the surprise. People with MD widely report that daydreaming interferes with sleep. But in a pre-registered diary study of 126 people, MD did not predict worse sleep the following night. Sleep loss, though, did predict more ordinary mind-wandering the next day. So protecting sleep still protects your focus.

scenes.head: Shame and isolation feed each other
scenes.say: Shame and isolation reinforce each other. Researchers call daydreaming and social isolation a two-way street: daydreaming leads to withdrawal, withdrawal to loneliness and shame, and those to more daydreaming. During lockdown, probable sufferers even had fewer online relationships.

scenes.text: MD's strongest online link is *problematic social media use*, perhaps because it lets people curate an ~idealised self~.
scenes.note: In 437 mostly male adults: MD went with celebrity worship and a desire for fame
scenes.say: For a creator, the most relevant link is social media. MD's strongest online link was with problematic social media use, perhaps because social media lets people manage their identity in line with an idealised self. In 437 Hungarians, mostly men, MD went together with celebrity worship and a desire for fame. All of this is correlational, and nobody has studied short-form video and MD directly.

scenes.head: Success fantasies: two things that feel alike

items: Vivid, pleasant images of the dream future

scenes.say: Now, success fantasies. Gabriele Oettingen's research separates two things that feel alike. Positive expectations are a judgement that you are likely to succeed. Positive fantasies are vivid, pleasant images of the desired future. Expectations predicted high effort and good results. Fantasies predicted the reverse: less effort and worse results.

scenes.head: Job seekers, two years later (83 graduates)
items: Most positive fantasies about landing a job
scenes.say: In one study, 83 German students rated their fantasies about graduating and landing a job. Two years later, those with the most positive fantasies had sent fewer applications, received fewer offers, and earned lower salaries. The same pattern held for romantic crushes, recovery from hip surgery, and weight loss.

scenes.bigl: blood pressure: energy drops after positive fantasy
scenes.text: Students who fantasised about an ideal week felt *less energised* and ~got less done~ a week later. Fantasy lets you ‘mentally consummate’ the goal.
scenes.say: Experiments show how. Positive fantasy lowered systolic blood pressure, a marker of physical energy, by 1.73 points, while a questioning fantasy raised it slightly. Students who fantasised about an ideal week felt less energised right away, and got less done a week later. In the researchers' words, positive fantasies let people mentally consummate a desired future, so effort feels unnecessary. The drain was bigger when the need was more pressing.

scenes.head: The mood effect flips over time
scenes.say: The mood effect also flips. Positive fantasies went with fewer depressive symptoms at the same moment, but predicted more depressive symptoms up to 7 months later, partly through lower grades. Fantasies also bias you toward looking at a goal's upsides over its downsides, which leads to worse decisions.

scenes.head: The remedy: WOOP (mental contrasting)
items: Outcome: picture the best result, briefly
Obstacle: the inner one, e.g. ‘I escape when editing gets boring’
Plan: if the obstacle shows up, then I…
scenes.say: There is an evidence-based remedy. Mental contrasting with implementation intentions, known as WOOP, pairs the wish with the obstacle and a plan. Wish, outcome, obstacle, plan. Across 21 studies and nearly 16,000 people, it improved goal attainment, with a small but reliable effect, and a larger one when done with another person. Oettingen's participants did not have MD, so applying this to MD is an inference, but a close one. We will build a full WOOP in chapter nine.

scenes.head: Excitement as a trigger (untested)
items: Good news: a view spike, a lead
Fantasy elaborates it, music lifts it
You ‘consume’ the success in your head
Less energy for the real next step
scenes.say: Your pattern includes excitement as a trigger. No study has tested this, so treat it as plausible but unproven. Good news, like a view spike or a new lead, brings excitement and an expected reward. The fantasy elaborates the reward, music lifts it further, and you consume the success in your head. Energy for the real next step drops, and that last link is the only one with experimental support. In favour of the idea: strong emotion of either kind pulls thought inward, and people with MD score high on reward sensitivity. Against it: in diaries, positive emotion did not predict next-day MD.

scenes.head: Your pattern vs the evidence
items: Starts when work gets uncomfortable: criteria, procrastination research, experiments
Music to amplify it: 36 of 41 say music deepens it
The session gets ruined: episodes run long
Active when not working too: a stable, trait-like pattern
Success fantasies: less energy, worse outcomes
Bedtime and idle time: solitude feeds it
Verdict: close match, but not a diagnosis
scenes.say: Put together, your pattern lines up with the evidence almost point for point. It starts when work gets uncomfortable, which matches the criteria and the procrastination experiments. You use music to amplify it, as 36 of 41 people in the music study described. The session gets ruined, because episodes run long. It is active when you are not working too, which fits a stable, trait-like pattern. Excitement as a trigger is plausible but untested. Success fantasies carry the most cost for someone building a business. And bedtime and idle time are prime territory, because solitude feeds it. A close match, but not a diagnosis.

scenes.text: Self-screening over-identifies MD by about *40 percent*. If ADHD, anxiety, depression or OCD symptoms sound familiar, ~get them checked~.
scenes.say: Two cautions. A close match to the criteria is not a diagnosis, because self-screening over-identifies MD by around 40 percent in population studies. And the conditions that most often travel with MD, inattentive ADHD, anxiety, depression and obsessive compulsive symptoms, are worth getting checked by a professional if any of them sound familiar.
What is the difference between a positive expectation and a positive fantasy, and which one predicts effort?
scenes.sayA: An expectation is a judgement that you are likely to succeed. A fantasy is a vivid image of the dream outcome. Expectations predict effort. Fantasies drain it.
scenes.a: Expectation: a judgement of likely success. Fantasy: a vivid dream image. Expectations predict effort.

scenes.say: Many people with MD say it wrecks their sleep. What did the diary study actually find?
scenes.sayA: MD did not predict worse sleep the next night. But poor sleep predicted more mind-wandering the next day.
scenes.a: No next-night sleep effect. But poor sleep raised next-day mind-wandering.
